question: Tell me about a time your team was spending so much time improving that deadlines were slipping. How did you restore the balance?

raiseTranscript.text: We were refactoring a service module for weeks and missed a feature deadline. I tracked my time and saw 60% on improvements. I brought it up in standup and suggested we cap refactoring at 20% per sprint.
My lead agreed, we shipped the feature on time, and kept smaller cleanups going. Learned to flag tradeoffs earlier.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time your team was spending so much time improving that deadlines were slipping. How did you restore the balance?
Role: junior dev on 4-person service team
Situation: 3 weeks of refactoring pushed feature slip by 5 days
Action: tracked time, proposed 20% cap in standup, aligned with lead
Outcome: feature shipped, small cleanups continued
Quote: 'I flagged the tradeoff in standup instead of just working on it'
Follow-up: What happened after? -> Lead agreed, learned to flag earlier
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Better than yesterday for a junior. The candidate owned their own time allocation and surfaced the issue to the lead rather than continuing unchecked. They restored balance by proposing a concrete cap that let both delivery and incremental improvement happen. The story shows clear learning from the slip and coachability in accepting the lead's input. Biggest strength is individual ownership of the tradeoff without waiting for escalation.

lowerTranscript.text: We kept polishing the code and the deadline just moved. I mentioned it once but the team kept going.
Did you do anything else to get back on track?
Not really, I just did what the team was doing.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time your team was spending so much time improving that deadlines were slipping. How did you restore the balance?
Role: junior dev
Situation: polishing caused slip but no personal action
Action: mentioned once, then followed team
Outcome: deadline moved, no balance restored
Quote: 'I just did what the team was doing'
Follow-up: Did you do anything else? -> No further steps
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Better than yesterday for a junior. The candidate observed the slip but took no ownership to restore balance beyond a single mention. No evidence of learning or adjusting their own work to protect delivery. The response shows passive behavior rather than the expected individual accountability at this level. Biggest gap is lack of any proactive step to rebalance improvement and deadlines.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams were stuck in a refactor loop on shared infra and missed two quarterly milestones. I ran a retro, set a 15% tech-debt allocation with the other lead, and tracked it in our planning tool.
We hit the next two milestones and still reduced incidents 30%. The other team adopted the same rule.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time your team was spending so much time improving that deadlines were slipping. How did you restore the balance?
Role: senior on platform team influencing adjacent team
Situation: refactor loop caused two missed quarterly milestones
Action: ran cross-team retro, negotiated 15% allocation, added tracking
Outcome: next milestones hit, 30% fewer incidents, other team copied the rule
Quote: 'I set the allocation with the other lead and tracked it'
Follow-up: How did that affect delivery? -> Hit milestones and spread practice
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Better than yesterday for a senior. The candidate used cross-team influence to define a sustainable allocation instead of letting improvement consume all capacity. They produced measurable delivery recovery plus a reusable practice the other team adopted. The story shows clear metrics and long-term leverage rather than one-off heroics. Biggest strength is restoring balance at the team boundary while raising the standard for both groups.

lowerTranscript.text: The team was deep in refactors and we missed dates. I told them we needed to ship but they kept prioritizing improvements.
What did you change in planning or process?
I raised it in the next planning meeting but the pattern continued.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time your team was spending so much time improving that deadlines were slipping. How did you restore the balance?
Role: senior
Situation: refactors caused missed dates
Action: verbal reminder in planning, no structural change
Outcome: pattern continued
Quote: 'I told them we needed to ship but they kept prioritizing improvements'
Follow-up: What did you change in planning or process? -> Only verbal reminder
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Better than yesterday for a senior. The candidate identified the imbalance but relied on verbal reminders without creating any enforceable process or metric. No evidence of influence across the team or lasting change. The response lacks the expected senior-level ownership of planning mechanics and cross-team coordination. Biggest gap is absence of any mechanism that actually restored balance.

raiseTranscript.text: Our org was allocating 40% to tech debt reduction and slipping three major launches. I reset the portfolio process to require explicit debt-vs-feature trade-off reviews at the VP level and tied it to quarterly OKRs.
Launch velocity recovered within two quarters while debt stayed under control; we later used the same model for two acquired teams.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time your team was spending so much time improving that deadlines were slipping. How did you restore the balance?
Role: exec overseeing multiple teams
Situation: 40% debt spend caused three missed launches
Action: introduced VP-level trade-off reviews and OKR linkage
Outcome: velocity recovered in two quarters, model scaled to acquisitions
Quote: 'I reset the portfolio process to require explicit trade-off reviews'
Follow-up: What was the longer-term result? -> Recovered velocity and scaled practice
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Better than yesterday for an exec. The candidate diagnosed an org-level allocation problem and introduced a durable governance change that protected both delivery and improvement. The intervention produced measurable recovery and was adopted beyond the original scope. The story demonstrates strategic judgment on trade-offs and long-term leverage rather than short-term fixes. Biggest strength is embedding balance into the operating system so the organization stays calibrated going forward.

lowerTranscript.text: Engineering was over-investing in improvements and launches slipped. I asked the teams to focus more on features.
Did you change any org process or incentives?
I sent guidance but left the existing planning process unchanged.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time your team was spending so much time improving that deadlines were slipping. How did you restore the balance?
Role: exec
Situation: over-investment caused launch slips
Action: sent guidance to focus on features
Outcome: no process change, pattern likely persisted
Quote: 'I asked the teams to focus more on features'
Follow-up: Did you change any org process or incentives? -> No, left planning unchanged
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Better than yesterday for an exec. The candidate recognized the org-level imbalance but applied only lightweight guidance without altering incentives, reviews, or planning mechanics. No evidence of the strategic trade-off decisions or scalable mechanisms expected at this level. The response shows reactive direction rather than durable system change. Biggest gap is failure to institutionalize balance at the portfolio or OKR layer.

diagnostic.junior: Individual time tracking and local proposal
Simple percentage cap suggested in standup
diagnostic.exec: VP-level trade-off reviews tied to OKRs
